The Case for a Unicameral Congress: Why America Should Abolish the Senate

Introduction

The United States Senate, once called "the world's greatest deliberative body," has become an antiquated institution that frustrates the democratic will of the American people. Created as a compromise to convince smaller states to ratify the Constitution, the Senate now stands as a structural barrier to effective governance and equal representation. By converting to a unicameral legislature based solely on population, America could streamline lawmaking, eliminate minoritarian gridlock, and create a government that truly represents the principle of one person, one vote.

The Representation Crisis

The Senate's equal representation formula has created a democratic crisis unprecedented in American history. Wyoming's 580,000 residents have the same Senate representation as California's 39 million—meaning a Wyoming voter has roughly 67 times more senatorial influence than a Californian. This isn't a minor imbalance; half the U.S. population is now represented by just 18 senators, while the other half controls 82 seats.

This disparity violates the fundamental democratic principle that all votes should count equally. When the Constitution was ratified, the population ratio between the largest and smallest states was approximately 12:1. Today it exceeds 68:1, a gap the Founders never envisioned or intended. The Supreme Court ruled in Reynolds v. Sims (1964) that state legislatures must follow "one person, one vote"—yet the U.S. Senate remains exempt from this basic democratic standard.

Partisan and Geographic Distortion

The Senate's structure doesn't just dilute representation—it systematically skews political power. Because low-population states are disproportionately rural and conservative, the Senate provides structural advantages to one ideological coalition over others. Democratic senators have represented a majority of Americans in most recent sessions, yet Republicans have frequently controlled the chamber.

This means legislation supported by representatives of most Americans routinely dies in the Senate. Popular reforms on issues from gun safety to voting rights to climate policy have passed the House only to languish because senators representing a minority of citizens can block action. This isn't democracy protecting minority rights; it's minority rule.

Legislative Gridlock and Inefficiency

The bicameral system requires legislation to pass two chambers with different constituencies, creating multiple veto points that paralyze government. This might have seemed wise to the Founders as a check on hasty action, but in modern practice, it produces only dysfunction.

Consider the legislative process: A bill must pass House committees, the full House, Senate committees, the full Senate, then reconciliation if versions differ, requiring yet another vote in each chamber. Each stage offers opportunities for obstruction. Add the filibuster—a Senate-specific rule requiring 60 votes for most legislation—and passing meaningful laws becomes nearly impossible.

A unicameral legislature would eliminate this redundancy. One chamber, one vote, clear accountability. Nations with unicameral systems, including New Zealand, Denmark, Sweden, and Finland, demonstrate that single-chamber parliaments can deliberate thoughtfully while acting decisively.

Accountability and Clarity

The bicameral structure obscures political accountability. When legislation fails, blame diffuses between chambers. Members of Congress can symbolically vote for popular measures knowing the other chamber will kill them, allowing posturing without consequences.

A unicameral system would create clear responsibility. Voters could directly judge their representatives' actions without confusion about which chamber blocked which priorities. This transparency would enhance democratic accountability and reduce cynical theatrical voting.

Economic and Administrative Efficiency

Maintaining two legislative chambers is expensive and wasteful. The Senate employs thousands of staff members, operates duplicate committee structures, and consumes resources that could serve citizens better elsewhere. While cost alone shouldn't determine constitutional structure, unnecessary expense adds insult to the injury of anti-democratic representation.

Historical Anachronism

The Senate was designed to represent state governments in an era when state legislatures selected senators and states were viewed as semi-sovereign entities. The 17th Amendment (1913) made senators directly elected, fundamentally changing their role but preserving the anti-democratic allocation formula.

This creates an institution with confused identity: no longer representing state governments, but not truly representing people equally either. It's a historical relic that persists through inertia, not because it serves contemporary democracy.

The Comparison with Other Democracies

Nearly half of all democratic nations employ unicameral legislatures, and they function well. The idea that effective governance requires two chambers is not supported by comparative evidence. Moreover, federal systems like Austria and South Korea manage regional representation without giving equal legislative power to dramatically unequal populations.

Even countries with bicameral legislatures typically make their upper chambers weaker than the U.S. Senate. Britain's House of Lords can only delay, not veto, legislation. The Senate's veto power over all legislation and appointments is exceptional—and exceptionally anti-democratic.

Addressing Counterarguments

"Small states need protection from large states": This assumes a conflict of interest between states based purely on size, which rarely reflects political reality. Californians and Texans don't vote as unified state blocs. Political divisions follow ideological, economic, and cultural lines that don't align with state boundaries. The real division the Senate protects is rural vs. urban, not small state vs. large state.

"The Senate encourages deliberation and prevents rash action": Deliberation doesn't require two chambers—it requires good procedural rules. A unicameral legislature can have extensive committee review, debate periods, and supermajority requirements for constitutional matters. The Senate doesn't add thoughtfulness; it adds obstruction.

"Bicameralism is a crucial check and balance": The American system has many checks and balances: federalism, separation of powers, judicial review, and the presidential veto. These mechanisms would remain. The question is whether this particular check—requiring legislation to pass two chambers with radically different representation formulas—serves democracy or frustrates it.

"This would require a constitutional amendment, which is impossible": Difficulty is not an argument for accepting injustice. Many necessary reforms seemed impossible until they weren't. The amendment process is challenging, but defending an indefensible institution because change is hard represents intellectual surrender.

A Vision for Reform

A unicameral Congress would consist of the House of Representatives, expanded to ensure adequate representation. Each member might represent 500,000 citizens, creating a roughly 660-member chamber. Proportional representation or multi-member districts could ensure diverse viewpoints while maintaining population equality.

This reformed Congress could modernize its rules: requiring only majority votes for most legislation, maintaining supermajority thresholds for constitutional amendments and treaty ratification, and implementing robust committee systems for thorough policy development.

Conclusion

The United States Senate is an 18th-century solution to 18th-century problems, now creating 21st-century crises of representation and governance. It grants disproportionate power to a geographic minority, creates unnecessary legislative gridlock, and violates the democratic principle of political equality.

Abolishing the Senate wouldn't weaken American democracy—it would fulfill it. A unicameral Congress based on equal representation would be more responsive, more accountable, more efficient, and more legitimate. It would ensure that the people who elect our government are actually the people it serves.

The question isn't whether we can afford to make this change. The question is whether we can afford not to. As the representation gap widens and legislative dysfunction deepens, the democratic cost of preserving the Senate grows unsustainable. It's time to complete America's democratic evolution and create a legislature that truly represents the principle that all citizens are created equal.

Title: A Case for Unicameralism: Why the United States Should Abolish the Senate

Introduction
The bicameral design of the United States Congress is deeply ingrained in the nation’s political DNA, with the House of Representatives granting proportional representation and the Senate granting equal standing to each state, regardless of population. Such a structure may have been a necessary compromise during the nation’s founding, but it now poses several obstacles to the principles of democracy and efficient governance. In a modern society that places increasing emphasis on equality and responsiveness, it is worth examining whether the Senate’s design serves as an impediment to progress rather than a safeguard of liberty. Moving toward a unicameral legislature—where all representatives are elected proportionally—could streamline lawmaking and eliminate the overrepresentation of smaller states, ultimately leading to more equitable and democratic governance.

  1. The Historical Context and Original Intent
    A. Revolutionary-Era Context
    The creation of the Senate in 1787 was primarily a compromise to accommodate and placate smaller states concerned about being overshadowed by larger states in the new national government. At a time when slavery existed, and when the original Thirteen Colonies held starkly different economic and political realities, this arrangement was seen as essential to ensure ratification of the Constitution.

B. Evolution Over Time
Over two centuries later, the nation’s population and state lines have shifted dramatically. State sizes vary significantly, and disparities in population cannot be dismissed as trivial matters of geography. Upon reflection, the Founders themselves recognized that the Constitution should evolve to suit modern realities; it is only natural, then, to consider whether the Senate still serves the purpose for which it was originally designed—or if it has become a roadblock to fair representation.

  1. Overrepresentation of Smaller States
    A. Disproportionate Power
    One of the most evident criticisms of the Senate is its equal representation of states regardless of population. This arrangement means that a senator from Wyoming, representing fewer than 600,000 residents, wields the same vote as a senator from California, representing nearly 40 million people. Consequently, smaller states hold a disproportionate share of power that can skew federal policy and funding priorities.

B. Impact on Policy Outcomes
Legislation that reflects the interests and concerns of a relatively small segment of the population can be advanced or blocked altogether by a minority in the Senate. For instance, measures on health care, social reforms, and other large-scale economic packages can be stymied by senators who represent only a fraction of the population. This structural imbalance fosters discontent throughout the country, as a majority of Americans may be thwarted by a legislative mechanism that privileges smaller states.

C. Tension with Democratic Principles
Democracies are built on the principle of “one person, one vote.” While the Senate was never explicitly meant to follow that principle, modern sensibilities accentuate the unfairness of disproportionately powerful Senate seats. It is increasingly difficult to justify a system that allows millions of people’s preferences to be undone or ignored by senators elected by far fewer voters.

  1. Ineffectiveness and Gridlock
    A. Duplication of Work
    Lawmakers and researchers often lament the legislative “ping-pong” between the House and Senate. Proposals can be passed easily in one chamber but face a slog of committee hearings, filibusters, and arcane procedural hurdles in the other. The repeated cycles of back-and-forth negotiations consume valuable time and taxpayer money. Abolishing the Senate would eliminate this dual-chamber negotiation, enabling a more direct legislative process.

B. Filibuster and Other Procedural Blockades
The filibuster—a rule allowing seemingly endless debate unless a supermajority decides to cut it off—has been a key source of gridlock in the Senate. In practice, any determined minority can indefinitely stall legislation, preventing decisions on vital issues like climate change, health policy, and constitutional protections. A unicameral legislature, unencumbered by Senate-specific rules, would be less prone to these procedural impediments, resulting in a more nimble and responsive Congress.

C. Reduced Legislative Fatigue
When significant public policy proposals are introduced, they frequently get bogged down in congressional deadlock. By removing a chamber prone to partisan obstruction and drawn-out debates, the legislative process could become significantly more efficient. This efficiency could inspire renewed public trust in the institution, as people see swifter action on issues that matter most.

  1. Toward a More Representative Government
    A. Proportional Representation as the Guiding Principle
    A primary virtue of a unicameral national legislature is that representation would be determined solely by population, taking the best features of the House of Representatives and applying them to the entire lawmaking process. In this model, each citizen’s vote would carry equal weight. Simplifying the legislative structure to a single body could bring more clarity to where representatives stand on key issues, holding them directly accountable to voters in their districts or at-large constituencies.

B. Inclusivity and Voter Engagement
A unicameral legislature could boost political engagement by making government workings more transparent and easier for voters to follow. One set of representatives, one voting process, and a single forum for debate: these conditions can reduce confusion, enhance media coverage, and encourage more citizens to interact with their representatives—resulting in sharper accountability and improved responsiveness to public opinion.

C. Balance of Powers with the Executive and Judiciary
Critics may argue that removing the Senate erodes checks and balances; however, both the judiciary and the presidency remain robust counterweights in the federal government. Moreover, the checks and balances system is not solely reliant on two legislative chambers—it spans multiple branches of government and includes judicial review, executive veto power, and constitutional constraints on legislation. A well-defined unicameral legislature would still be subject to these checks and balances, ensuring that no single branch wields excessive authority.

  1. Economic and Administrative Efficiency
    A. Fewer Elected Officials, Lower Costs
    Operating two separate legislative bodies is expensive. Each chamber requires its own budget for staff, offices, and procedural logistics. Abolishing the Senate would inherently save taxpayer dollars by reducing duplicative efforts, allowing a leaner, more cost-effective administrative structure.

B. More Rapid Policy Implementation
Major policy bills such as infrastructure legislation, defense budgets, and social spending packages often linger for months—or even years—caught in bicameral wrangling. A unicameral legislature would enable policy to be enacted more swiftly, responding to economic or humanitarian crises in a timely way. This streamlined approach can produce quicker results in disaster relief, recession responses, or sudden global emergencies, improving the country’s overall resilience.

C. Opportunities for Innovation
By simplifying the legislative process, the government can experiment with innovative policy solutions on voting methods, civic engagement programs, and transparency measures. Rather than being stifled by the constraints of a bicameral system, a single legislative body can focus on brainstorming and testing creative ideas to address modern challenges.

  1. Counterarguments and Rebuttals
    A. Preservation of Federalism
    Some insist that the Senate is crucial to ensure federalism and the autonomy of individual states. Yet federalism does not necessarily require granting smaller states disproportionate power at the national level. States will continue to govern their own affairs under the Tenth Amendment, and local governance structures will remain intact. A unified legislature can still pass regulations that apply equally to all citizens, without compromising the ability of states to administer certain policies within their borders.

B. Fear of Tyranny of the Majority
Opponents argue that a unicameral legislature risks majoritarian overreach, neglecting minority viewpoints. However, diversity within the House of Representatives demonstrates the varied ideologies and regional interests that come together in one chamber. Constitutional checks, such as the Bill of Rights and judicial review, offer further protection to minority voices. In fact, a unicameral legislature may be more transparent, giving every group a clear path to voice concerns in a single, well-defined arena.

C. Tradition and Constitutional Rigidity
The U.S. Constitution has evolved through amendments and reinterpretations over centuries, yet many traditions remain entrenched. The Senate is one of these longstanding institutions. Tradition, however, should not preclude necessary reform. Other democratic nations, such as New Zealand and much of Scandinavia, have successful unicameral legislatures. There is no fundamental reason that bicameralism remains necessary for the United States in the 21st century.

Conclusion
Abolishing the United States Senate and moving toward a unicameral legislature constitutes a seismic shift in American governance. Nevertheless, the structural advantages are clear: this reform promises more equitable representation, faster legislative action, and reduced costs for taxpayers. The current system, while historic, often exacerbates division and allows a minority of states to wield disproportionate influence. Transitioning to a single legislative chamber that reflects population-based representation would more faithfully align with democratic principles. It would also lessen the notorious legislative gridlock that hinders progress on vital national issues—from health care to economic stability to infrastructure. While debate over such a dramatic change would undoubtedly be impassioned, it is precisely that passionate engagement with questions of governance that can lead to a more egalitarian and effective United States.

  2. The Filibuster and Minority Rule: While not in the Constitution, the filibuster effectively requires a 60-vote supermajority to pass most legislation in the Senate.   3. Outdated Original Purpose: The Senate was designed as a check on the popular will and to protect the interests of states as sovereign entities (the Connecticut Compromise). Critics argue that after the 17th Amendment established the direct election of senators, and especially after the Civil War established the supremacy of the federal government, this original purpose is obsolete. States are no longer sovereign entities but administrative units of a single nation.

Supposed Benefits of a Unicameral Congress

1. Fairer Representation and Democratic Equality

This is the central benefit. A single-chamber Congress would almost certainly be apportioned strictly by population, just as the current House of Representatives is.

  • One Person, One Vote: Every American's vote would have equal weight in electing the national legislature. A vote in Delaware would count the same as a vote in Texas. This would align the U.S. system with the democratic principle followed by most other modern democracies and its own state legislatures (Nebraska excepted).
  • Shift in Political Power: Legislative power would shift to reflect where Americans actually live—in large states and metropolitan areas. Policies would theoretically need to appeal to a national, popular majority rather than to a geographic coalition of small states.

2. Increased Efficiency and Reduced Gridlock

A unicameral system would streamline the legislative process dramatically.

  • Elimination of Redundancy: The current bicameral system requires a bill to pass through two separate, independent bodies with different rules, calendars, and political compositions. This process is slow, fraught with obstacles, and requires complex conference committees to reconcile different versions of the same bill. A single chamber would debate and vote on a bill only once.
  • Faster Response to Crises: A more streamlined legislature could theoretically respond to national emergencies, economic shifts, and technological changes with greater speed and agility, unencumbered by a second, often more deliberative and obstructive chamber.
  • Accountability: With only one house responsible for passing legislation, it would be clearer to voters who is responsible for success or failure. There would be no opportunity for one chamber to blame the other for inaction.

3. Reduction of Special Interest Influence

The Senate, with its smaller membership and longer terms, is often seen as more susceptible to lobbying and the influence of well-funded special interests. A larger, more populous chamber would, in theory, dilute the power of any single lobbyist or industry group, as they would have to influence a much broader and more diverse body of representatives.

4. Fiscal Efficiency

Maintaining two separate legislative bodies with their own staff, committees, and facilities is expensive. Consolidating into a single chamber would reduce the operational costs of Congress, saving taxpayer money.

Significant Counterarguments and Practical Hurdles

It is crucial to understand why this is unlikely to happen and the arguments for retaining the Senate.

  • Constitutional Near-Impossibility: Abolishing the Senate would require a constitutional amendment. Article V of the Constitution states that "no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate." This means every single state would have to agree to give up its equal representation—an insurmountable political hurdle, as the small states would never vote away their own power.
  • The Value of Deliberation: The Senate was designed to be a "cooling saucer" for the passions of the House. It forces slower, more deliberate consideration of legislation, preventing radical swings in policy based on temporary popular fervor.
  • Protection of Minority Interests: While it protects small-state minorities, critics of unicameralism argue this can be a good thing.   • The Example of Nebraska: Nebraska is the only state with a unicameral legislature. While it operates efficiently, it is nonpartisan and much smaller than the federal government, making it a difficult comparison. It has not necessarily been immune to gridlock or special interest influence.

Conclusion

The push to eliminate the U.S. Senate is fundamentally a push for a majoritarian democracy, where national policy is determined strictly by the national popular will. The supposed benefits are greater democratic fairness, streamlined efficiency, and reduced gridlock. However, the American system was intentionally designed not to be a pure majoritarian democracy. It was built on a framework of checks, balances, and compromises meant to protect minority interests (in this case, the states as political units) from the potential tyranny of the majority. The debate over the Senate is, therefore, a timeless debate about the very nature of American democracy: Is it a nation of people, or a union of states? The current system attempts to be both.

Abolish the Senate: The Case for a Unicameral Congress

A Democratic Imperative for the Twenty-First Century

The United States Senate is, by design, one of the most anti-democratic institutions in the Western world. It grants Wyoming's 576,000 residents the same legislative power as California's nearly 40 million. It allows a minority of senators representing barely a third of the American population to block legislation supported by overwhelming majorities. It was born of a political compromise meant to preserve the power of slaveholding states and small agrarian colonies, and in the centuries since, it has calcified into a bottleneck that frustrates the popular will, paralyzes the legislative process, and renders American governance sluggish and unresponsive. The time has come to seriously reckon with a provocative but increasingly necessary proposition: the United States should abolish the Senate and convert Congress into a single, proportionally representative legislative chamber. Doing so would streamline the lawmaking process, eliminate the grotesque overrepresentation of small states, restore the principle of political equality, and bring American democracy in line with the standards it claims to champion around the world.

I. The Senate Was a Compromise, Not a Principle

Defenders of the Senate often speak of it with reverence, as though it were an expression of some timeless democratic ideal. It was not. The Senate was the product of the Connecticut Compromise of 1787, a backroom deal struck between large and small states that nearly destroyed the Constitutional Convention before it began. Delegates from smaller states like Delaware and New Jersey refused to join a union in which their influence would be proportional to their populations. Delegates from larger states like Virginia and Pennsylvania considered equal representation in a legislative chamber to be a violation of basic republican principles. James Madison himself—the so-called Father of the Constitution—argued passionately against equal state representation, calling it unjust and illogical. He lost the argument not on the merits but because the small states held a credible threat of walking away from the convention entirely.

The compromise was just that—a compromise. It was a concession to political necessity, not a reflection of democratic theory. The Founders themselves were deeply divided on the question, and many of the most intellectually rigorous among them regarded the Senate's structure as a defect to be tolerated rather than a virtue to be celebrated. To treat the Senate as sacrosanct is to confuse an expedient bargain among eighteenth-century elites with an eternal truth about governance. The conditions that necessitated the compromise—a fragile confederation of quasi-sovereign colonies uncertain about whether union was even desirable—have long since disappeared. The United States is not a loose alliance of independent republics. It is a single nation of over 330 million people, and its legislature should reflect that reality.

II. The Mathematics of Misrepresentation

The most damning indictment of the Senate is arithmetical. Each state, regardless of population, sends two senators to Washington. This means that a voter in Wyoming has roughly 68 times the senatorial representation of a voter in California. A voter in Vermont has approximately 25 times the representation of a voter in Texas. The twenty-six least populous states, which together contain less than 18 percent of the American population, control a majority of the Senate's seats. This is not a minor distortion at the margins of an otherwise fair system. It is a foundational structural inequality embedded in the heart of American governance.

Consider what this means in practice. Legislation that commands the support of senators representing a vast majority of the American people can be killed by senators representing a small fraction of it. The filibuster exacerbates this problem, but even without it, the basic arithmetic of the Senate ensures that the preferences of rural, less populated states are systematically amplified while the preferences of urban, densely populated states are systematically suppressed. The Court carved out an exception for the Senate only because the Constitution explicitly mandates its composition, not because the arrangement is just. If we were designing a government from scratch today, no rational democrat would propose giving Idaho and New York identical representation in a legislative chamber. The Senate survives not because it is defensible but because it is entrenched.

III. The Legislative Graveyard

Beyond its representational failures, the Senate is a catastrophically inefficient legislative institution. Its rules and traditions—the filibuster, the hold, the privileging of unanimous consent, the baroque committee system—have transformed it into what critics rightly call "the place where good legislation goes to die." The House of Representatives, for all its flaws, is at least capable of passing bills with majority support in a reasonably timely fashion. Laws would move from committee to floor to the president's desk in a single, transparent process. Senate debates are often perfunctory, with members reading prepared statements to a nearly empty chamber before casting votes determined in advance by party leadership. Nothing about the number two—two chambers rather than one—is inherently more deliberative. Nebraska has operated with a unicameral legislature since 1937, and its lawmaking process is widely regarded as more transparent, more efficient, and more accountable than those of its bicameral counterparts.

On the international stage, numerous thriving democracies operate with unicameral legislatures—Sweden, Denmark, Finland, New Zealand, Israel, and South Korea among them. These nations are not less democratic or less deliberative than the United States. If anything, their legislative processes are more responsive and more representative. The American insistence that bicameralism is essential to good governance is a parochial assumption unsupported by comparative evidence.

Defenders of the Senate sometimes argue that small states need protection from the "tyranny of the majority," that without equal representation in the Senate, large states would ride roughshod over the interests of smaller ones. This argument fails on multiple levels.

First, it assumes that states are monolithic entities with coherent, unified interests that need representation as states. They are not. The political divisions within California or Texas are far more significant than the political divisions between Wyoming and Vermont. A rancher in rural California has more in common politically with a rancher in Wyoming than with a software engineer in San Francisco. State lines are largely arbitrary—historical accidents of colonial charters, territorial acquisitions, and congressional decisions about how to subdivide the frontier. They do not correspond to meaningful communities of interest that require special institutional protection.

Second, the argument proves too much. If small political units deserve equal representation to prevent domination by larger ones, then the same logic should apply within states. Should each county in New York have equal representation in the state legislature, regardless of population? The Supreme Court said no in Reynolds v. Sims, recognizing that such arrangements violate the equal protection of the laws. The principle does not magically become valid when applied at the federal level.

Third, the practical effect of small-state overrepresentation is not to protect vulnerable minorities from oppression—it is to give disproportionate power to a demographic group (rural, predominantly white Americans) that already exercises outsized influence through the Electoral College, gerrymandered House districts, and the federal judiciary. The Senate does not protect the powerless. It amplifies the power of a group that is already overrepresented in virtually every other institution of American government.

Critics will immediately object that abolishing the Senate would require a constitutional amendment, and that Article V of the Constitution appears to make this nearly impossible by stipulating that "no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate." This is a serious practical obstacle, but it is not a principled argument against the reform. The difficulty of achieving a change says nothing about its desirability. Moreover, constitutional scholars have debated whether this provision could itself be amended through a two-step process—first amending the restriction, then amending the Senate's composition—or through a constitutional convention. The point of a persuasive essay is not to draft the legislation but to build the moral and intellectual case for change. If Americans become convinced that the Senate is unjust and dysfunctional, they will find the constitutional mechanisms to reform it, just as they found mechanisms to abolish slavery, extend suffrage to women, and establish the direct election of senators themselves—all changes once considered impossibly radical.

Others will argue that a unicameral legislature would concentrate too much power in a single body, inviting hasty or tyrannical legislation. But the American system has no shortage of checks on legislative power. The president retains the veto. The judiciary retains the power of constitutional review. The Bill of Rights constrains what any legislature may do, regardless of its structure. A unicameral Congress operating within the existing framework of separated powers, judicial review, and constitutionally protected rights would not be an unchecked body—it would simply be a more efficient and representative one.

VII. A Democratic Renewal

Abolishing the Senate is not merely a structural reform. It is a moral imperative. The legitimacy of democratic government rests on the principle that each citizen's voice carries equal weight. The Senate violates this principle in the most fundamental way possible, granting some citizens dozens of times more legislative influence than others based on nothing more than where they happen to live. It is a relic of an era when the nation was a fragile experiment, when states were quasi-sovereign entities, and when the franchise was limited to white, property-owning men. We have outgrown every other aspect of that founding bargain. We should outgrow this one as well.

A unicameral Congress, proportionally representative of the American people, would be more democratic, more efficient, more transparent, and more accountable. It would end the spectacle of a minority of the population holding the majority hostage. It would accelerate the legislative process without sacrificing deliberation. It would force the government to be responsive to the nation as it actually is—a diverse, urbanizing, interconnected society of 330 million people—rather than to a phantom nation of separate, coequal sovereignties that ceased to exist in any meaningful sense generations ago.

The Senate was a necessary compromise in 1787. It is an indefensible anachronism in the twenty-first century. It is time to let it go.

The measure of a democracy is not how faithfully it preserves the compromises of the past, but how honestly it confronts the injustices those compromises created. Abolishing the Senate would be the most significant democratic reform in American history since the Nineteenth Amendment. It is long overdue.

My fellow Americans,

Why does a voter in Wyoming have sixty-eight times the representation in the United States Senate as a voter in California?

I. The Senate Is an Affront to Democratic Equality

We hold these truths to be self-evident — that all men and women are created equal. That is the creed carved into our national identity. It is the idea that has inspired revolutions around the world. And yet it is an idea that the United States Senate violates every single day of its existence.

The Senate does not represent people. It represents land. It represents arbitrary lines drawn on a map. It gives two senators to the 580,000 residents of Wyoming and two senators to the nearly 40 million residents of California. It means that the 50 senators representing the least populous states can constitute a majority — while representing barely 18 percent of the American population.

Let me say that again: 18 percent of the population can control a majority of the Senate.

This is not a feature. This is a distortion. This is a funhouse mirror held up to the will of the people, and we have been told to call it "checks and balances."

The Founders themselves were divided on this question. James Madison — the very father of the Constitution — opposed equal representation in the Senate. He called it a defect. He argued passionately for proportional representation in both chambers. He understood, even then, that giving equal voice to unequal populations was not balance — it was injustice dressed in the clothing of compromise.

Madison lost that argument in 1787. But his reasoning has only grown stronger with time. The population disparities between states today are vastly greater than anything the Founders could have imagined. And the consequences are vastly more destructive.

But this isn't just a philosophical argument. This is about the real, tangible harm that the Senate inflicts on this nation every single year.

Think about the legislation that has died in the Senate. Think about the bills that passed the House of Representatives — the chamber that actually reflects the will of the majority — only to be buried in the Senate graveyard. Gun safety measures supported by 90 percent of Americans. Infrastructure investments. Climate action. Immigration reform. Electoral reform. Bill after bill after bill, passed by the people's House, only to be strangled by an institution that answers to geography rather than to human beings.

And it's not just the structure. It's the rules. The filibuster — that arcane, anti-democratic procedural weapon — means that in practice, you don't need 51 senators to block legislation. You need only 41. Forty-one senators, potentially representing as little as 11 percent of the American population, can hold the entire nation hostage.

Eleven percent. Blocking the will of eighty-nine percent.

This is not governance. This is paralysis by design.

A unicameral Congress would strip away these layers of obstruction. One chamber. One set of rules. One clear line of accountability between the people and their representatives. When the people speak, their voice would not have to navigate a labyrinth of procedural traps and structural inequities. It would be heard.

"But wait," the defenders of tradition will say. "Surely we need two chambers! Surely we need the 'cooling saucer' of the Senate to prevent hasty legislation!"

We are not drowning in reckless laws. We are drowning in inaction. We are choking on gridlock. The American people are crying out for solutions to problems that have festered for decades, and the Senate sits there — slow, unaccountable, insulated from the popular will — and calls its dysfunction deliberation.

And let us dispense with the myth that unicameral legislatures are some radical experiment. Nebraska has operated with a single legislative chamber since 1934 — and it functions. It functions well. New Zealand, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, South Korea, Portugal — nations with thriving democracies, stable governments, and robust protections for minority rights — all operate with unicameral legislatures.

These nations prove what common sense should tell us: you do not need two chambers to have good governance. You need one good chamber — transparent, accountable, and representative of the people it serves.

A well-designed unicameral Congress could incorporate robust committee systems, deliberation periods, supermajority requirements for constitutional matters, and strong protections for civil liberties — all without the redundancy, dysfunction, and anti-democratic distortion of a second chamber that represents acres instead of people.

Let us be honest about something that polite political discourse often avoids: the Senate was not designed to be democratic. It was designed to protect the interests of small states — and, let us not forget, of slaveholding states — against the will of the majority.

Senators were not even elected by the people until 1913, when the Seventeenth Amendment finally wrested that power from state legislatures. For 124 years, the Senate was an explicitly anti-democratic institution. The Seventeenth Amendment was a recognition that the original design was flawed — that the people deserved a direct voice.

But the amendment only went halfway. It gave us the right to vote for our senators, but it left in place the fundamental inequality: two per state, regardless of population. It democratized the process without democratizing the structure.

And that structural inequality has consequences that fall hardest on the most vulnerable. Urban communities, communities of color, immigrant communities — the populations that are growing fastest and that are most concentrated in large states — are systematically underrepresented in the Senate. Rural, predominantly white, less populous states wield outsized power.

This is not an accident. This is the architecture of the institution functioning as designed. And if we believe — truly believe — in the equal dignity and equal voice of every American citizen, then we must have the courage to say: this design has failed the test of justice, and it must be changed.

V. "But the Founders—"

I can already hear it. The reverent invocation of the Founders, as if the men who wrote the Constitution were prophets rather than politicians.

Let me be clear: I revere the Founders for their boldness, not for their perfection. These were men who had the audacity to look at the existing order and say, "We can build something better." They did not cling to tradition for tradition's sake. They broke with tradition. They experimented. They innovated. They created a framework and then — crucially — they built into it the capacity for amendment, because they knew, they knew, that future generations would see what they could not.

The Constitution is not a sacred text to be preserved in amber. It is a living framework — one that has been amended twenty-seven times. We amended it to abolish slavery. We amended it to grant women the right to vote. We amended it to establish the direct election of senators. Each time, we moved closer to the democratic ideal that the original document only gestured toward.

Abolishing the Senate would not betray the Founders' vision. It would fulfill it.

It would complete the unfinished work of building a government that is truly of the people, by the people, and for the people — not of the acreage, by the state lines, and for the politically entrenched.

VI. The Path Forward

Yes, this is a monumental undertaking. Yes, it requires a constitutional amendment — perhaps the most ambitious one in our history. I will not pretend otherwise.

But consider what we would gain:

  • True proportional representation. Every American's vote carrying equal weight in a single national legislature.
  • Legislative efficiency. No more ping-ponging bills between two chambers, no more conference committees watering down the people's will, no more using one chamber to kill what the other has built.

A unicameral Congress would mitigate this issue, as legislative power would be directly tied to the number of constituents represented.
